title: Sapphire Hill - Private LLM Onboarding Sync
summary: Intro discovery between Redwood AE/SE and Sapphire Hill engineering/security to scope private/VPC onboarding for LLM inference. Main constraints: EU data residency, strict egress IP allowlist, transit gateway usage, and key management integration. Agreed next steps: share security pack + sample network diagram, run a short latency/cost pilot on Dedicated vs Private, and schedule an infra checklist workshop.
topics: KMS/HSM integration and encryption at rest
Pilot scope: throughput/latency targets and test harness
action_items: Maya Patel (Redwood): Send SOC2 + network diagram + sample ip allowlist format by 2026-06-12
Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE): Prepare benchmark run script and recommended instance/quantization profile by 2026-06-17
Priya Desai (Sapphire Hill): Confirm list of permitted egress IPs and legal team contact by 2026-06-15
next_steps: Redwood to share security pack and VPC peering diagram
Schedule 2-hour infra workshop (SE + Sapphire Network team)
Plan 1-week pilot comparing Dedicated vs Private with 10k qps simulated prompts
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-10
Time: 15:00 PT / 23:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Priya Desai (CTO, Sapphire Hill), Carlos Mendes (Network Eng), Ayesha Khan (Security Lead)

[00:00] Maya Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood, and with me is Liam, our solutions engineer. How are we doing?
[00:08] Priya Desai: Good, thanks. Busy day but excited to dig in — we want to make sure the private onboarding path works for our EU clients.
[00:15] Liam O'Connor: Awesome. Quick agenda, we'll cover networking options—peering, private endpoints, egress—then security/KMS, and outline a pilot. Feel free to interrupt.
[00:23] Carlos Mendes: Quick note, we operate primarily in eu-west-1 and eu-central-1, and we have a transit gateway that handles connectivity to our analytics clusters. We need to understand where Redwood would sit and how routing/egress would look.
[00:35] Maya Patel: Got it. Are you leaning to Dedicated reserved capacity or a fully private VPC deployment? Or undecided?
[00:42] Priya Desai: Undecided. Our risk team prefers private VPC with customer-managed routing, but cost and ops are concerns. If Dedicated gives us the same controls but simpler ops, we might consider it.
[00:55] Ayesha Khan: From security, the big ones are: SOC2 compliance, audit logs export, SSO/SAML, and importantly our KMS (AWS KMS with a CMK we control). We can't have keys managed by a third party.
[01:12] Liam O'Connor: That's common. For Redwood Private we support customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations in the private control plane; keys live in your account. For Dedicated, we can offer encryption with customer KMS too, but there's a different network topology—Dedicated is still Redwood-managed infra but with isolated pools.
[01:30] Carlos Mendes: Can you sketch the differences network-wise? For example, do you use VPC peering, transit gateway attachments, or PrivateLink/private endpoints? We want to minimize NAT egress changes.
[01:45] Liam O'Connor: Sure—high-level: Private (VPC) deployment usually attaches to your transit gateway; compute nodes live in your account or in a connected account and we install endpoints. We support either VPC peering in smaller setups or TGW attachments for enterprise scale. PrivateLink (AWS PrivateLink) is an option for control-plane APIs but doesn't always suit high-throughput token streams.
[02:08] Priya Desai: So PrivateLink for control traffic, TGW for the data plane?
[02:12] Liam O'Connor: Exactly. For high throughput and predictable latency, TGW/transit attachments are preferred so you can route between your VPCs without hairpinning. PrivateLink is better for management plane calls or where customers restrict routing.
[02:26] Carlos Mendes: Our egress policy requires a stable set of IPs so our security team can allowlist them. How do you handle egress IPs for private deployments?
[02:35] Maya Patel: For private deployments, egress IPs can be under your control if compute lives in your account. If we manage infra in Dedicated, we provide a published set of egress IPs and can set up SNAT via your NAT Gateway or a transit egress point. We also support static egress via NAT Gateway in the customer's account.
[02:56] Ayesha Khan: Important — we can't accept ephemeral outbound IPs. We need a monthly schedule of any IP changes and ideally a CIDR block we can allowlist.
[03:08] Liam O'Connor: Understood. We can commit to an allowlist file format and change window notifications. For Dedicated customers we typically publish a /28 block per region; for Private in-customer compute you'd control it.
[03:22] Priya Desai: What about multi-region residency? We need EU-only processing for certain customers. Does Redwood support region gating so inference never leaves EU?
[03:30] Liam O'Connor: Yes—Redwood supports routing policies and region pinning. In Private you choose where the compute is deployed. For Hosted and Dedicated we'd use region-aware routing and fallbacks; but for strict EU-only stance, Private with compute in eu regions is the recommended path.
[03:45] Carlos Mendes: Great. Any compliance docs we can send to legal?
[03:49] Maya Patel: We'll send SOC2, ISO attestation if requested, data flow diagrams, and a sample network diagram showing TGW attachments and PrivateLink. We'll also include an example allowlist CSV.
[03:59] Ayesha Khan: Also we need logging/audit details — how long logs retained, where they live, and access controls.
[04:06] Liam O'Connor: Audit logs can be pushed to your S3 with SSE-KMS, or integrated with your SIEM via Kinesis/CloudWatch. Retention is configurable; we can mirror logs to your account for sovereignty.
[04:20] Priya Desai: Sounds good. On performance, our latency SLO is 120ms p95 for short chat completions (~512 tokens). Can you hit that from eu-west?
[04:31] Liam O'Connor: With a local eu instance pool and optimized kernels we typically see ~60–100ms p95 for small requests on our optimized models. With quantization and KV caching enabled you can reduce token time further. For strict p95 targets we'll recommend a benchmark run in your network to measure e2e latency including your client-side overhead.
[04:53] Carlos Mendes: For the benchmark, we need details on the test harness. Are you providing the generator or do we run a local agent?
[04:59] Maya Patel: We'll provide a light-weight test script that simulates concurrency and a benchmark harness that can run from your VPC. Liam will prep that.
[05:08] Ayesha Khan: Regarding keys, our legal insists on customer-managed CMKs and HSM-backed keys. Any limitations?
[05:14] Liam O'Connor: No major limitations—Private deployment allows for CMKs in your account. For Dedicated, we can integrate with customer KMS through cross-account roles; HSM integration might need additional architecture but it's doable. We'll include specifics in the packet.
[05:28] Priya Desai: We have an internal GPU fleet talk — one point: latency/cost tradeoffs. If we self-host, ops cost is high but maybe cheaper per-token. How do you present cost for Dedicated vs Private vs Hosted?
[05:41] Maya Patel: We'll send a comparative estimate: hosted per-token pricing, Dedicated with committed monthly cost (plus usage patterns), and Private with infra + Redwood platform fee. We'll model a 6-month forecast for expected qps. Also, Redwood Optimize can recommend batching/quant profiles to lower unit cost.
[06:00] Carlos Mendes: Network-specific: NAT gateway SNAT port exhaustion is a concern at scale. Do you support multiple SNATs or egress IP slices?
[06:09] Liam O'Connor: Yes—best practice is to allocate multiple NAT Gateway IPs and use port address translation strategies; we can advise on SNAT scaling and recommend using TGW egress with deterministic NAT if needed.
[06:23] Priya Desai: Are there any known pitfalls with transit gateway attachments and cross-account routing? We use accounts-per-team model.
[06:31] Liam O'Connor: Cross-account attachments require proper IAM principals and route propagation. We typically work with infra teams to set up a shared-services account for attachments, or we can deploy per-account stacks. We'll enumerate required CloudFormation/IaC templates so your infra team can review.
[06:50] Maya Patel: Can we talk about timeline? What is your expected pilot date?
[06:55] Priya Desai: Ideally mid-July—two week pilot starting ~2026-07-13. Legal review may take 2–3 weeks, infra work another week. So we'd need docs soon.
[07:07] Maya Patel: We'll target sending the security pack and network diagram by Friday, 2026-06-12. Liam will follow with the benchmark harness and recommended instance profile by 2026-06-17.
[07:19] Carlos Mendes: For the pilot, we want a minimal setup that doesn't require full TGW changes—can you support a VPN/Direct Connect tunnel to a Redwood-managed account for the pilot?
[07:28] Liam O'Connor: For pilots, yes. We can accept a VPN or Direct Connect to a Redwood-managed test account. That lets you validate latency and routing without touching production TGW configs. If the pilot meets expectations we'll move to a more permanent TGW or in-account deployment.
[07:44] Ayesha Khan: One more — data retention for prompts/responses: we need controls to disable retention or ensure retention in our account only.
[07:52] Liam O'Connor: We support configuration flags to disable retention and ensure logs/outputs are stored only in your buckets. We'll include data retention policy options in the packet.
[08:03] Priya Desai: Are there API auth patterns we should use for mutual TLS or token-based? Some of our services prefer mTLS for east-west calls.
[08:12] Liam O'Connor: We support token-based API keys, OAuth, and mTLS for private control-plane endpoints. For high-security flows mTLS is recommended — we'll document examples.
[08:25] Maya Patel: Any blockers from your side today?
[08:29] Priya Desai: Nothing blocking, just we need that security packet and specific IP allowlist format, plus a legal contact who will review contracts.
[08:37] Carlos Mendes: I'll pull current NAT IPs and share them. Also need a contact from Redwood who'll own the infra workshop.
[08:44] Maya Patel: Liam will own the infra workshop. I'll be the commercial point and send pricing.
[08:49] Priya Desai: Great. Can you also include any runbooks for failover/fallback? We want to understand graceful degradation—if a region is down do requests failover to another region and what is the data residency implication?
[09:03] Liam O'Connor: We'll include a runbook. Short answer: we support routing policies that can prefer EU-only endpoints; fallback can be disabled for strict residency. If you allow fallback, we log it and you can set alerts.
[09:18] Ayesha Khan: One small nit — our legal asks about indemnity around model outputs, do you have standard language?
[09:24] Maya Patel: We'll include standard terms plus a note about model responsibility disclaimers; legal can propose redlines.
[09:31] Priya Desai: Ok, thanks. When can we schedule the 2-hour infra workshop? Week of June 22 looks promising for us.
[09:38] Liam O'Connor: I'm available June 23 or 24 afternoon PT — we'll propose times in the follow-up.
[09:45] Maya Patel: Summarizing next steps: Redwood sends SOC2/security pack + sample network + allowlist format by 6/12; Lily — sorry Liam will send benchmark harness by 6/17; Priya will provide egress IPs and legal contact by 6/15; schedule workshop week of 6/22. Pilot aim mid-July.
[10:10] Priya Desai: That matches our notes. Thanks, everyone.
[10:14] Carlos Mendes: Thanks.
[10:16] Ayesha Khan: Thank you.
[10:18] Maya Patel: Thanks all — we'll follow up with the packet and calendar invites.

End of meeting.

Notes on transcript: transcription contains occasional mistranscriptions (e.g., "Lily" mistaken for "Liam" in passing), filler words, and some speaker attribution smearing typical of automated call transcriptions.
